analysis.one_liner: Lets farmers and independent repair shops legally bypass digital locks to diagnose, maintain, and repair farm equipment.
analysis.headline: The right-to-repair bill has sat untouched in the House Judiciary Committee since March 2026, with zero cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal copyright law makes it illegal to bypass the digital locks manufacturers put on their products. This bill would carve out an exception for farm equipment, so farmers and independent repair shops could legally get past electronic locks to diagnose, maintain, or fix tractors and other digital farm machinery. It was introduced by one representative, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers, who would no longer risk violating copyright law just to fix their own equipment or hire an independent mechanic instead of waiting for a dealer. Independent repair shops and makers of aftermarket tools and diagnostic software would also gain a legal market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmers and independent equipment repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Federal copyright law (Section 1201 of title 17) bans bypassing digital locks on products; the bill would make it legal to get past those locks for the purpose of diagnosing, maintaining, or repairing digital farm equipment [S2].

The bill would also legalize building, importing, or selling the tools, software, and parts needed to do that repair work, so independent shops could actually offer the service instead of only dealers [S2].

In practice this matters because modern tractors and combines depend on embedded electronics to function, and today a farmer who bypasses a manufacturer lock — even to fix a breakdown during planting or harvest — risks legal liability [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Farm equipment manufacturers, chiefly companies like John Deere, which collect revenue from exclusive dealer-performed repairs, proprietary diagnostic software, and factory-authorized parts. They would face competition from independent repair and aftermarket parts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealer networks

drawbacks.text: The bill lifts legal restrictions but requires nothing of manufacturers: it does not force them to sell parts, publish repair manuals, or license diagnostic software, so repairs could remain difficult in practice even after locks are legally bypassable [S2].

Copyright holders argue that legalizing circumvention tools risks the tools being used for other purposes, like copying protected software; the bill's definition of covered equipment — anything agricultural that depends on embedded digital electronics — is broad [S2].
Neither manufacturers nor safety regulators have weighed in through any committee hearing or report, so safety and warranty questions around third-party repairs are unresolved in the record [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farmers, the upside is real but limited: the bill removes the legal risk of fixing machines that are locked down with software, which matters most during short planting and harvest windows when dealer service queues are long. But it is a half-measure — it does not compel manufacturers to provide parts, documentation, or diagnostic tools, so equipment makers could still make independent repair slow or impractical. On the other side, manufacturers lose a captive repair market but keep their design and sales business.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Representative Victoria Spartz introduced the Farm Freedom to Repair Act on March 5, 2026 [S1] [S4].

The bill would amend federal copyright law so bypassing digital locks on farm equipment is legal for diagnosis, maintenance, and repair, and so tools for that repair can be legally made and sold [S2].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, which is the only action taken on it [S4].
No other member of the House has cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor count is zero — and no committee action or vote has followed [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm equipment manufacturers keep their exclusive grip on repairs for now: with no cosponsors and no committee movement, nothing threatens their dealer-only repair model, while farmers continue to depend on dealers for fixes their own machines are electronically locked against.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm equipment makers keep their repair monopoly

for.name: Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: The committee his panel controls has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — since it was referred in March 2026.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill with zero cosponsors from either party, and no votes have occurred, so no partisan pattern exists yet.

industries.note: These companies lock their machines with software and channel repairs through their own dealers and proprietary tools, which is a significant revenue stream. If the bill passed, farmers and independent shops could legally bypass those locks, ending the manufacturers' repair monopoly on machines farmers already own.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and aftermarket tool and parts makers
industries.note: The bill would legalize building and selling the diagnostic tools, software, and parts needed to service digital farm equipment, creating a market that copyright law currently blocks. Farmers would gain more repair options and likely lower prices.

Dealers currently hold the exclusive franchise on service for locked equipment. Independent competition for repair work would cut into that service revenue, though dealers could still compete on speed and parts availability.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced by a single member with no cosponsors almost never reach a floor vote, and the Judiciary Committee has shown no movement. Unless repair advocates or farm groups build cosponsor support, the bill is likely to sit until this Congress ends and expire without a vote.
